items.target: Testing Claude on real-world electronics design
items.text: anthropic-research published: Testing Claude on real-world electronics design
items.title: Testing Claude on real-world electronics design
items.content:
01
Reasoning through geometric problems
A little over a year ago, we began testing how well Claude could design basic electronic circuits. We
collaborated with Diode Computers
,
1
a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards, to train Claude on simple tasks—for example, on reading a chip’s datasheet and working out which parts a chip needs in order to run. The models we experimented with back then couldn’t reliably lay out a circuit board; they also struggled to design components that fit together. Now, Claude can both design and prototype electronic hardware from start to finish.
Engineering an electronic device requires working through many complex steps and practical constraints. You have to not only design and simulate a circuit board, but also reason about the board’s physical layout and how it will behave, model the mechanical components, and write firmware—all while keeping track of which parts are readily available and what a factory is set up to build.
To see how newer Claude models have improved in this area, we collaborated with Diode again, this time asking Claude Fable 5.2 to design three electronic devices: a speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub, and a handheld virtual pet. With minimal prompting, Claude was able to use geometric reasoning to lay out each circuit board, anticipate manufacturing constraints, and make sure its designs would work within them. It revised its own work, modeled its designs in computer-aided design (CAD) software, and, finally, directed human engineers to build prototypes that worked without any fixes to their circuitry.
For each design, we began by giving Claude a simple prompt that outlined what kind of device to build and its main hardware requirements. The prompt for the speakerphone, for example, asked for “a puck that plugs into a computer over USB-C and includes microphones and a speaker, supporting Bluetooth with a PCB antenna.” Claude proceeded to write the device’s specifications, draw clean visual schematics, choose where to place the components on a printed circuit board (PCB), route the copper connections between them, design a 3D-printable enclosure, code the firmware, and prepare a parts list. Diode assembled the circuit boards and ran the firmware, under Claude’s direction. The final result was a prototype of a speakerphone that still works after weeks of use.
Claude went through a similar process to build the voice-assistant hub and the virtual pet, and both are also still in good working order. Because the devices are early prototypes, we don’t yet know how they’ll hold up with continued use or whether they would pass commercial certifications.
The three devices built from Claude’s designs, from left to right: a battery-powered handheld pet, a home voice-assistant hub, and a USB speakerphone. Claude engineered the electronics and the enclosures and wrote firmware for each one.
Reasoning through geometric problems
The most substantial difference between Fable 5.2 and the models we used in our earlier tests was in how well Fable 5.2 reasoned through complex geometric problems, such as where to place components on a circuit board and how to route the copper connections between them.
Earlier models had struggled to decide how to arrange basic components—placing supporting parts too far from the chips they served, for example, or orienting connectors incorrectly. Fable 5.2, by contrast, produced more compact, practical layouts. It routed the most important connections first: those that carry high-speed signals or high currents, or that are sensitive to noise. For example, for the voice-assistant hub, Claude started by routing the USB and Ethernet connections, which transmit signals along pairs of tracks—thin strips of copper on the board. It routed one pair of tracks at a time, keeping the two tracks in each pair the same length and correctly spaced. It also added tuning patterns—small zigzags that lengthen a track so that signals arrive at the same time—and arranged the parts of the power supply to make it more efficient.
To demonstrate how much better Fable 5.2 is than earlier models at laying out circuit boards, we asked Diode to run PCB Gym—an internal benchmark that scores models based on how well they can place components and reroute connections on board designs whose layouts have been removed. Fable 5.2 scored 69% on the benchmark, compared with 25% for Fable 5 (Figure 2). It also performed better on
BenchCAD 2.1
, a public benchmark that tests whether models can rebuild 3D parts, assemblies, and circuit boards from engineering drawings and rendered images. Fable 5.2 scored 83.5%, nearly double the score of its predecessor, Claude Fable 5.1.
Scores plotted against total API cost for recent frontier models on Diode PCB Gym, a benchmark that instructs models to place components and route connections on circuit boards whose layouts have been removed.
Revising designs
Earlier models rarely revised their own work when designing PCB layouts, even when it became clear that their placement choices would never let them finish routing the connections. Over the past year, Diode designed many boards with these models that were 95% complete but still unusable.
When Claude noticed one of its designs wasn’t working, it would change course without being prompted to do so. For instance, when designing the speakerphone’s circuit board, which has four layers of copper, it reassigned signals to different pins on two of the chips. This allowed the tracks under the speakerphone’s touch-sensitive controls to stay on a single layer without crossing one another. Later, when the back of the board became too crowded, Claude swapped the signals on interchangeable pins and laid out a whole corner of the board again, rather than patching the problem with extra jumps between layers.
And when placing tracks in its design file for the voice-assistant hub, Claude noticed that the copper connections were “getting too tangled to trace visually” and reasoned, “I should just rip these traces [tracks] and start fresh.” It proceeded to delete and reroute copper connections dozens of times until it found an arrangement that worked.
The routing for the voice-assistant hub before and after Claude reorganized the connections. Left: the microphone’s power track (blue lines) loops around the ground ring at the sound port, a front-side track (red) crosses the ring, and a via—a small hole that connects layers of copper—is placed between the microphone’s pads. Right: the same area after Claude rerouted the power track, with the ring clear and grounded. Claude’s reasoning for redoing the version on the left: “That’s risky placement under a bottom-port MEMS mic, even if clearance is technically fine, so I want to redo the local routing cleanly for both identical mic footprints.”
Using software and documentation
When a design decision for one of the devices depended on the details of a particular part, Claude often checked that part’s datasheet—a technical document published by the manufacturer. When asked whether the handheld pet would work without a battery, Claude read the charger’s datasheet and answered that it would run on USB power but predicted that the charging light would flicker, because the charger keeps recharging a small capacitor in the battery’s place.
2
To route the connections on the voice-assistant hub, Claude started with the design software Diode provided, which let it run the router (a tool for drawing tracks) built into KiCad, a widely used circuit board design program. KiCad’s router drew one track at a time between two points Claude chose. But the hub had long tracks running from a 100-pin connector, and Claude judged that routing these one by one would take too much step-by-step guidance.
Instead, Claude wrote its own router: an algorithm that divides the board into a grid and searches it to find a clear path for each track. Within about half an hour, Claude had a router that could lay each long track in roughly a second. When Claude spotted an audio clock track running too close to the Ethernet tracks, it adjusted the router to leave more room around sensitive tracks.
Keeping track of constraints and downstream effects
Decisions made in one part of a design have downstream effects, which Claude kept track of. While designing each device’s enclosure, it wrote code to check that a 3D model of the circuit board would fit inside the enclosure without any components colliding. For example, it found that the speakerphone’s board couldn’t be lowered straight into the enclosure, because the mute switch would hit the back wall. Claude worked out that the board would fit if it was tilted by about 25 degrees during installation. It tested this in its 3D model and added the step to the assembly instructions.
When designing the enclosure for the voice-assistant hub, Claude calculated that a 25 mm-long microphone port—the opening that lets sound reach the microphone—would resonate near 3.4 kHz. That is “right in the voice band,” it reasoned, “which is not ideal though still usable for voice assistant purposes. A better approach is a wedge-shaped enclosure that’s tall at the rear and steps down low at the front.” The wedge shape shortened the ports to about 10 mm, which raised the resonant frequency to about 8.9 kHz, at the very edge of the range used for speech. Claude also wrote firmware for the speakerphone that dims its ring of LED lights as the audio becomes louder, to keep the device under the electrical current limit Claude had designed into the board.
Claude’s designs for the home voice-assistant hub and the finished prototype. Claude wrote the code that modeled the case in CAD, laid out the circuit board, and wrote the firmware.
Designing for real-world manufacturing
In electronics design, engineers have to work within the constraints of the real world. That is, they have to make sure a factory can actually make the thing they want to build. They do this by running two kinds of checks: design-for-manufacturing (DFM) checks, which compare a circuit board’s geometry with the factory’s manufacturing limits, and sourcing checks, which confirm that their distributors have the parts in stock.
Claude ran these checks itself and sorted the results into problems that needed fixing and flags it could ignore. Its checks for the voice-assistant hub flagged six slivers of solder mask (the protective coating on a circuit board) as too thin to manufacture. Claude fixed them by widening the openings in the solder mask, without moving any parts. The checks also flagged a connection between two grounds (shared return paths for electrical current) as an error, because the automated checker hadn’t recognized that the connection was deliberate. Claude correctly reasoned that it wouldn’t affect performance and ignored the flag.
Diode manufactured all three boards directly from Claude’s design files, without any back-and-forth over adjustments. Factories and engineers often have to work through multiple rounds of manufacturing changes, and the Diode team told us they were surprised that they didn’t have to do this with Claude.
Layer 1: front
Layer 2: inner 1
Layer 3: inner 2
Layer 4: back
The speakerphone’s four copper layers. The dashed circle marks the touch wheel, where copper electrodes sense the user’s finger. Moving a track from one layer to another requires drilling a hole in the board, and under the touch wheel, that hole would go through an electrode. To avoid this, Claude kept each signal track under the wheel on a single layer, and it chose the chips’ pin assignments so that those tracks wouldn’t need to cross one another. It also kept the area around the Bluetooth antenna (the zigzag at the top) clear of other copper and holes on every layer, so nearby metal wouldn’t weaken its signal.
Layer 1: front
Layer 2: inner 1
Layer 3: inner 2
Layer 4: back
The voice-assistant hub’s four copper layers. Claude added two areas of grounded copper to the power layer (green), directly behind most of the tracks on the back of the board that carry high-speed signals. This gives the signals a nearby return path, which helps reduce interference.
The speakerphone’s circuit board can’t be lowered straight into the enclosure, because the mute switch’s knob would hit the back wall (red). Claude worked out how to install the board by tilting it about 25 degrees and then swinging it flat, and added this step to the assembly instructions.
Limitations and next steps
All three of these devices are still prototypes: they haven’t been through electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing, or certification, and they weren’t designed for mass production. Since Claude wasn’t connected to test equipment or to the machines that make and assemble circuit boards, engineers at Diode had to physically build and test the prototypes. Even so, over the past year, Claude has improved substantially at reasoning through decisions about component placement and routing, and it can now design electronics with minimal human guidance and help people build the prototypes. Other models are making progress here, too: OpenAI recently
wrote about using its models
to design a handheld device. Work like this could help engineers build and test new hardware designs faster.
Next, we plan to investigate whether Claude can design denser, faster, and more complex boards, check them in simulation, and learn from measurements taken on the finished devices.
Footnotes
01
Anthropic has a commercial relationship with Diode.
02
This was one of the few instances where the Diode team prompted Claude (“Will it work if there is no battery?”). Overall, their prompting was minimal and limited to short directives (e.g., “clean up the schematic” and “continue”).
Authors & acknowledgements
Acknowledgements
This post is a collaboration between researchers and engineers at Anthropic, including Mike Cretella, Connor Jennings, and Brent Yi, and Craig Chen and the team at Diode Computers. Anthropic has worked with Diode electrical engineers on PCB design since 2025. Editorial support from Xander Balwit, Tom Chivers, Rebecca Hiscott, and Caitlin Love.

items.target: Vulnerability Analysis: CVE-2026-123158 “SSHole” – Critical Root Vulnerability in Alpine Linux Systems
items.text: denizhalil-blogs published: Vulnerability Analysis: CVE-2026-123158 “SSHole” – Critical Root Vulnerability in Alpine Linux Systems
items.title: Vulnerability Analysis: CVE-2026-123158 “SSHole” – Critical Root Vulnerability in Alpine Linux Systems
items.content:
Introduction
The cybersecurity landscape recently witnessed a highly critical vulnerability dubbed “SSHole” (CVE-2026-123158). This flaw represents a severe authentication bypass issue that primarily impacts lightweight, container-friendly operating systems like Alpine Linux. By exploiting an unintended collision between several independent security mechanisms, unauthenticated remote attackers can bypass SSH authentication entirely. In specific cloud environments, this seamlessly translates to immediate, unauthorized root access, making it one of the most critical threats to modern cloud infrastructure and containerized workloads. Because Alpine is the foundational base image for millions of Docker containers and Kubernetes deployments worldwide, the potential attack surface is staggering. Furthermore, the exploit leaves minimal traces in standard access logs, making post-incident forensic analysis incredibly challenging for security teams trying to identify unauthorized intrusions before massive data exfiltration occurs.
Learning Objectives
By reading this vulnerability analysis, you will be able to:
Grasp the foundational security concepts that inadvertently collided to create the SSHole vulnerability.
Understand the specific technical interaction between
musl libc
and OpenSSH.
Identify the exact system configurations and conditions that make an environment vulnerable.
Apply immediate mitigation techniques and permanent remediation steps to secure affected systems.
What is SSHole? A Critical Root Vulnerability in Alpine Linux Systems (CVE-2026-123158)
SSHole (CVE-2026-123158) is a critical authentication bypass vulnerability that emerges not from a single coding error, but from the dangerous overlap of three distinct security features. In Linux systems, user accounts that are disabled or do not have a password (meaning they should only be accessed via SSH keys) are securely marked with an asterisk (
*
) in the password field of the
/etc/shadow
file. Under normal circumstances, this mechanism guarantees that no text-based password can ever match the stored hash, theoretically locking the account down against brute-force attacks. However, the vulnerability occurs when OpenSSH’s defense mechanism against user enumeration timing attacks interacts poorly with a Denial of Service (DoS) protection feature built directly into the
musl libc
library. This obscure edge-case interaction essentially tricks the SSH daemon into believing that an attacker has successfully provided the correct password for a completely locked-down account, bypassing the cryptographic barrier entirely. The implications of this flaw are profoundly amplified in modern cloud architectures. Because administrators heavily rely on default accounts without passwords to streamline automated deployments and provisioning scripts, the attack surface expands dramatically. Once the authentication layer is bypassed, the system inherently trusts the rogue connection, paving the way for complete infrastructure compromise without a single valid credential.
It is classified as an Authentication Bypass vulnerability with a critical CVSS score of 9.8.
It specifically targets the flawed interaction between the
musl libc
cryptographic functions and OpenSSH’s internal daemon logic.
It primarily affects system accounts that have been explicitly disabled or locked using the
*
shadow hash indicator.
It requires absolutely no prior knowledge of the target system’s credentials, private SSH keys, or active user behavior.
+--------------+ +-------------------------+
| | 1. Send 257-byte password | |
| Attacker | ----------------------------> | OpenSSH Daemon |
| | | |
+--------------+ +-------------------------+
|
| 2. Pass input to crypt()
V
+------------------------------------+ +-------------------------+
| | <------ | |
| /etc/shadow File | 4. Match| musl libc |
| | '*' | |
| Account: alpine | with | 3. Reject oversized input,
| Password Hash: '*' | '*' | return '*' as error |
+------------------------------------+ +-------------------------+
|
| 5. MATCH FOUND!
V
[ Access Granted -> Root via doas ]
Technical Detail: How the Vulnerability Works
The mechanics of the SSHole vulnerability can be broken down into a sequence of events triggered by a meticulously crafted, anomalous login attempt. To prevent CPU exhaustion attacks, the
crypt()
function within the
musl libc
library is designed to reject passwords that exceed 256 bytes in length. When it encounters such a massive input, it refuses to process the expensive hashing algorithm and instead safely returns a single asterisk (
*
) as an error indicator to the calling application, aiming to drop the load immediately. Concurrently, OpenSSH is designed to prevent attackers from guessing valid usernames based on server response times. If an attacker tries to log into an invalid account or an account without a password, OpenSSH still performs a “dummy” password verification in the background using the password salt of another valid user on the system. This ensures that every login attempt takes the exact same amount of time, masking the existence of specific users and thwarting enumeration techniques.
The fatal collision happens when an attacker targets an account that has no password (like the default
alpine
user, which possesses a
*
in the
/etc/shadow
file). The attacker intentionally sends a password longer than 256 bytes. The
musl libc
library rejects the long password and outputs the error code
*
. OpenSSH’s faulty validation logic then blindly compares this returned
*
with the actual hash stored in the shadow file (which is also
*
). Because the two values perfectly match, OpenSSH interprets this as a successful cryptographic verification.
Trigger:
The attacker initiates a standard SSH connection but provides a manipulated password string exceeding the 256-byte limit.
Library Response:
The
musl libc
library intercepts the oversized string, aborts the hash calculation, and returns the
*
error token.
Daemon Logic:
OpenSSH proceeds with its timing mitigation routine, improperly comparing the returned error token directly against the
shadow
file entry.
Escalation:
Access is mistakenly granted to the default account, which subsequently leverages its pre-configured
doas
rules to instantly achieve root privileges.
Affected Software & Plugins
The scope of CVE-2026-123158 is heavily restricted by the specific architectural choices of the underlying operating system and its authentication daemons. Unlike widespread vulnerabilities that affect the ubiquitous
glibc
library, this flaw is strictly confined to systems that rely on the lightweight
musl libc
implementation. This makes Alpine Linux, Void Linux (the musl variant), and various embedded firmware solutions like OpenWrt the primary targets for this sophisticated attack vector. Furthermore, the vulnerability requires a very precise configuration state within the OpenSSH daemon itself. Systems utilizing Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) are naturally immune because PAM overrides and entirely replaces the faulty internal OpenSSH validation logic. The attack only succeeds in environments where basic password authentication is enabled, PAM is disabled, and the specific shadow file conditions are met simultaneously.
Operating systems utilizing
musl libc
instead of standard
glibc
(e.g., Alpine Linux, OpenWrt, Buildroot).
OpenSSH daemon versions prior to 10.6p2 that were compiled or configured without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) support.
System configurations explicitly allowing standard password authentication (
PasswordAuthentication yes
in the
sshd_config
file).
Systems containing at least one disabled or passwordless account (
*
) alongside at least one valid hashed account to facilitate the timing mitigation phase.
Conclusion
The SSHole vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) serves as a stark reminder that isolated security mechanisms can sometimes combine to create catastrophic systemic failures. It demonstrates how a Denial of Service protection rule in one underlying library and a timing attack mitigation feature in a network daemon can unwittingly collaborate to bypass authentication entirely. This “perfect storm” of overlapping logic flaws highlights the extreme complexity and fragility of modern software stacks. System administrators operating Alpine Linux or other
musl
-based systems must take immediate and decisive action to secure their infrastructure against this threat. To permanently remediate the issue, OpenSSH must be updated to version 10.6p2 or the subsequently patched version provided by the respective OS maintainers. Crucially, updating the software packages is not enough on its own; a full restart of the SSH daemon is mandatory to clear the vulnerable code from the active system memory. If immediate patching is not feasible due to strict production constraints or uptime requirements, administrators can apply a highly effective temporary mitigation by altering their SSH daemon configuration. By explicitly setting
PasswordAuthentication no
in the
sshd_config
file and relying strictly on cryptographic keys, the attack vector is completely neutralized. Ultimately, adopting a Defense in Depth strategy remains the best safeguard against such unpredictable, multi-layered vulnerabilities.

items.target: Migrating from React Native to UIKit in 87 Hours: Hollow Out the Data Layer, Then Invert the Host
items.text: innei published: Migrating from React Native to UIKit in 87 Hours: Hollow Out the Data Layer, Then Invert the Host
items.title: Migrating from React Native to UIKit in 87 Hours: Hollow Out the Data Layer, Then Invert the Host
items.content:
Lody iOS started out on Expo + React Native. By October, the chat timeline, composer, Live Activity, and Share Extension had all been rewritten in UIKit—roughly 61,000 lines of Swift alongside 37,000 lines of TypeScript. What remained of React Native was mostly routing and screen-level glue: navigation was split half in Expo Router and half in native code, and every build still ran through
expo prebuild
, Metro, and CocoaPods.
Repository
· innei-dev
527
lody-ios
Independent iOS client for Lody — native chat, sessions, and coding-agent collaboration on iPhone
Swift
On the night of October 24, I decided to remove React Native entirely and replace the remaining screens with UIKit one by one. On the morning of October 28,
#96
merged into
main
, deleting the RN runtime after roughly three and a half days (87 hours) across 482 files (+25,700 / −37,500 lines). I then spent the next three days reorganizing the directory structure around explicit dependency layers.
Whiteboard
Finishing the cutover in 87 hours was only possible because the real strangler-fig work had started six weeks earlier. Between early September and mid-October, diff rendering, the chat timeline, and the rich-text composer were extracted into standalone packages, followed by
cloud-runtime
on October 11. By the time the migration started on October 24, the app was already layered like this:
Whiteboard
In other words, React Native had already been hollowed out into a thin outer shell: the heavy UI primitives were standalone packages, and the data runtime had lived inside a Swift-owned offscreen
WKWebView
from day one. The migration came down to three questions:
Where should the cross-platform boundary live once coding agents make native UI cheap? How do you invert the host of a 100k-line app without freezing trunk? And when offline verification holds pixel diffs to 0.00026, which four regressions still slip through the cracks?
1. The Shifting Premise: Moving the Shared Boundary from UI to Data
We originally chose React Native with a future Android client in mind. The bet was to keep both the data layer and the UI abstraction in RN: React components would describe screen layouts, while iOS and Android would merely supply the underlying native views. When it came time to build Android, we would only need view implementations—neither the data layer nor screen structures would have to be rewritten.
Whiteboard
The left side shows that original bet; the right side shows where we landed. The shared cross-platform boundary moved down from UI to a headless data layer:
cloud-runtime
runs inside an offscreen WebView, iOS and a future Android client implement the same versioned contract, and each platform writes its UI natively.
Two shifts broke the original equilibrium. First,
coding agents collapsed the marginal cost of native UI
. Writing a separate UI per platform used to be the exact expense RN was meant to save. In this migration, the remaining screens were rewritten in batches alongside coding agents in three and a half days. Once the one-time cost of writing native screens drops that low, paying an ongoing abstraction tax to avoid it no longer pencils out.
Second,
the three-layer translation tax in navigation
. Navigation bars, toolbars, and sheets ultimately end up as UIKit, but in RN they had to pass through three layers of translation to get there:
Whiteboard
On the left, every layer maintains its own state and assumptions. As soon as iOS 26 glass styling, iPad split views, and iPhone Duo foldable layouts entered the picture, bugs clustered in the seams between layers (the gray annotations show a few issues hit while adapting for Duo). Our patch against
react-native-screens
started on September 10 and was revised 11 times before deletion. On the right, there is no middleman—each view controller owns its navigation items directly.
Each individual glitch was patchable, but every fix added another layer of state translation between RN and UIKit. On October 17, I got wide-screen layouts working for iPad and iPhone Duo in RN, and the result still felt rough. A week later, I decided to stop patching and go all-in on native.
2. The Strangler-Fig Inversion: Hollow Out First, Flip the Host Second
To swap out the host without halting feature work on
main
, we couldn't start by rewriting screens. We had to unwind a reverse dependency chain: six weeks of preparatory extraction to hollow out the shell, followed by three sequential locks once the cutover began.
Six Weeks of Prep: Stripping Out Heavy Views and Data Until Only Routing and Context Remained
The timeline below lays out the extractions between September 6 and October 24 across two tracks—the data layer and UI primitives:
The three heaviest UI subsystems went first: diff rendering (
dom-webview
), the chat timeline (ChatKit), and the rich-text composer (
lexical-swift
). They were already written in Swift or self-contained DOM bundles that RN screens simply mounted. When we later replaced screens one by one, the new UIKit view controllers imported those packages directly without having to untangle view logic mid-flight.
Repository
· Innei
3
ChatKit
UIKit chat primitives: streaming text reveal, attachment strip, glass surface. iOS 26, Swift 6.
Swift
The data layer was never inside RN to begin with. Swift owned an offscreen
WKWebView
where sync, local replicas, and retries ran; RN only ever received read-only projections for display. On October 11, that runtime and its protocol types were extracted into
@lody/cloud-runtime
.
Earlier, on September 8, the cloud code had already been split by domain into
auth
,
catalog
, and
send
—the exact three boundaries that would become Swift's
AuthSession
,
CatalogSession
, and
Outbox
on October 25. By the night of October 24, all RN held besides routing was the state inside five root Context providers.
Lock 1: Establish a Versioned Contract and Sink State into Swift
Why didn't day one touch a single screen? Because replacing screens incrementally required UIKit to own navigation first, turning each remaining RN screen into an independently hosted root view. Once screens become separate root views, React Context on a single root component can no longer span across them—so global state had to leave RN first. And for Swift services and native screens to talk to the offscreen runtime without going through RN, Swift and the runtime needed a formal contract.
Previously, Swift invoked the runtime by concatenating raw JS strings, which was tolerable when the RN host was the only caller. Now native screens needed to call the runtime directly—and a future Android host would need the exact same surface—so the very first commit on October 24 replaced string interpolation with a schema-driven contract:
The Zod schema in
cloud-runtime
became the single source of truth. Types for every platform are generated from it, and the host and runtime only exchange envelopes carrying a schema version (
v
) and instance generation (
gen
). Version mismatches fail the handshake immediately, and messages from stale WebView generations are dropped on sight. Swapping the host—or adding a new platform—never touches the runtime.
Over the next 23 hours, the five React Contexts on the RN root were consolidated into four single-owner Swift services. The left side shows the old RN root provider tree; the right side shows how both RN and UIKit screens read state afterward:
Each slice of state has a single owner in Swift. Remaining RN screens and new UIKit screens read the same synchronous JSON snapshot and subscribe to the same change event. Splitting screens into separate root views no longer affected shared state—and as a security bonus, long-lived Better Auth credentials now stayed strictly in Swift and Keychain without ever entering the JS context. By the evening of October 25, once
Outbox
landed in Swift and
CatalogProvider
was deleted, the root Context tree was empty.
Lock 2: Invert the Host so UIKit Wraps RN Screens
With state out of the way, Expo Router still owned navigation. As long as RN owned navigation, native views could only live as child components inside RN screens—we could never replace a whole screen. The pivotal move was inverting the host relationship: UIKit took over the window and navigation chrome, demoting the remaining RN screens into leaf views hosted inside UIKit containers. The diagram below shows the three stages of the host; this step moved us from left to center:
Whiteboard
In that middle transitional state, each unmigrated RN screen became an isolated surface backed by a single shared
RCTHost
. The outer UIKit container didn't care whether a destination was rendered by an RN surface or a native view controller, unlocking true screen-by-screen replacement without blast radius across pages. (Earlier on iPad, I had tried reparenting a mounted RN view into a different superview, which silently broke touch press handling; giving each screen its own surface avoided that trap entirely.)
The new UIKit shell went in behind a launch flag first. Compact iPhone navigation and regular-width iPad split navigation were wired up in turn; once both ran cleanly, Expo Router was deleted in the early hours of October 26—six hours from feature flag to router removal.
Lock 3: Cut the Umbilical Cord—Remove the RN Runtime and Build Chain
Once all remaining RN leaf screens were replaced with UIKit (covered in the next section), the app still booted through Expo's
AppDelegate
and every build still ran through
expo prebuild
and Metro.
#96
severed that final layer—moving from the center of the host diagram to the far right: a native
AppDelegate
/
SceneDelegate
boots
LodyApplication
directly, giving lifecycle, deep links, push notifications, and the share inbox native owners. The build pipeline flipped with it:
The
ios/
directory is no longer wiped and regenerated by
prebuild
; the Xcode project is generated deterministically from a committed
project.yml
via XcodeGen. React, Expo, Hermes, and the stack of
react-native-screens
patches were deleted together. Only the headless WebView runtime bundle continues to be built with
pnpm
—the one layer that never changed from start to finish.

· innei-dev/lody-ios

3. Deterministic Verification and Its Cracks: 0.00026 Pixel Diffs vs. 4 Escaped Regressions
Between October 26 and October 28, rewriting every remaining screen in UIKit within 48 hours—without breaking
main
—would have been impossible with manual QA. What made the blitz safe was an offline verification harness; what makes it interesting in hindsight are the four bugs that still escaped it.
Leaf-to-Trunk Replacement: Isolating Every Screen Behind a Single Service Seam
Once the UIKit shell was in charge, every native screen was built around the exact same decoupled structure:
A view controller's only I/O is a
service
closure. Production routes inject the
live
implementation (wired to
DataRuntime
,
Catalog
, and
Outbox
); Debug scenes inject a
scripted
implementation returning fixed fixtures. Both paths run the exact same view controller. Before flipping any screen, we registered an offline Debug scene and a
verify:ui
behavioral test that deep-linked straight into it—no login, no cloud, and no local agent daemon required—running the identical assertion suite before and after the swap.
With offline assertions in place, replacement proceeded mechanically from leaves to trunk. On October 26, all Settings sub-screens, Home, and Project screens moved first; that night, the complex Session screen was built in UIKit behind a Debug fixture. On October 27, the remaining screens were conquered in a stack of eight PRs (
#87
–
#94
): message editing, message details, tool details, permissions, PR view, and file browser, followed by flipping the production Session entry point to native and finishing Home and iPad navigation. On the morning of October 28,
#86
and the entire PR stack merged together.
Pull Request
· innei-dev/lody-ios

+
26846
−
18771
Innei
2 weeks ago
When
#96
deleted the RN runtime hours later, the offline UI suite ran directly against the pure native build. Across 20 screenshots of the new-session form compared pixel-by-pixel against the previous build, the maximum diff was
0.00026
.
Where the Harness Cracked: How 4 Regressions Escaped a 0.00026 Pixel Gate
Even with screenshot diffs pinned to the fourth decimal place and core flows working cleanly, four regressions still surfaced after cutover. Looking at them side by side is revealing—every single one lived on the seam between offline scripted scenes and the real runtime environment:
Whiteboard
The test entry point had no test of its own
: The Debug screen dispatches every offline scene, yet had no test case covering itself. After converting to UIKit, it regressed into an ungrouped flat list missing its navigation bar.
Build configuration skew (Debug vs. Release)
: Debug scenes were only registered under
Debug
and
UI Verify
build configurations, and automated checks never ran against
Release
. Long-pressing the Settings button in TestFlight builds triggered an unregistered route and crashed immediately.
Offline stubs bypassed the OS modal hierarchy
: During Device Flow sign-in,
SFSafariViewController
presents over the welcome screen; after authorization completed, dismissing closed only Safari while leaving the welcome screen stuck underneath. Because the "open browser" step in the offline fixture was a no-op stub, the real system modal stack was never exercised.
Static fixtures skipped async teardown races in the live runtime
: Opening a session from a push notification caused the previous screen's delayed
deinit
to close the session the new screen had just opened. Offline scenes fed synchronous scripted data without a live
DataRuntime
, so that cross-controller lifecycle race never fired under test.
4. Post-Merge Convergence: Freeze Paths During Cutover, Layer by Dependency After
Throughout the 87-hour sprint, I followed one strict rule:
never move files while changing behavior
. Keeping file paths frozen meant every commit was a pure implementation swap—easy to review and trivial to
git bisect
if something broke. The trade-off was that when
#96
landed, all 557 Swift files were still sitting inside the legacy Expo module directory, mixing view controllers, data sessions, and platform glue. Only after behavior was locked down did I put on the refactoring hat for three days of structural layering, again doing one thing per step:
Step 1: Move files without splitting code.
With RN gone,
apps/mobile
and the Expo module path were vestigial. All Swift sources were moved wholesale into a single Swift package,
LodyKit
, while dependencies switched from CocoaPods to SPM.
Step 2: Split along the
import UIKit
boundary.
Auth, catalog, outbox, the data runtime host, session models, and copy were extracted into
LodyData
—a module that never imports UIKit and compiles and tests in isolation. Whenever the data layer needs a platform side effect (opening URLs, requesting background execution time, showing a toast, presenting an auth browser, or writing a Share Extension snapshot), it calls the
LodyHost
protocol, which the top-level App target implements and injects.
Step 3: Flatten the project hierarchy.
The repository root became the Xcode project root, eliminating the
apps/
wrapper. Finally, the remaining UI code in
LodyKit
was folded back into the App target—the App was its only consumer, while views shared with the Share Extension moved into
Shared/UIKit
as direct source references. Keeping a separate UI package only added ceremony around access control, so the App target is now organized directly into
Application
,
Navigation
,
ViewControllers
,
Views
,
Services
, and
Platform
.
The resulting dependency graph flows strictly in one direction—the lower a layer sits, the less it knows about UI:
Whiteboard
The repository root is the Xcode project root, generated from the committed
project.yml
; the generated
Lody.xcodeproj
is never edited by hand.
Takeaways for Anyone Planning a Similar Migration
Looking back, the critical factor wasn't how fast UIKit views could be written—it was respecting a strict sequence of dependency locks where each step unlocked the physical precondition for the next:
Start by deciding
which layer actually deserves to be shared
. React Native's cross-platform leverage lives in UI; once coding agents make platform-native UI cheap to write, it pays to push the shared boundary down into a headless data runtime behind a versioned contract. Extract heavy UI primitives first, sink shared state out of RN, and then invert the navigation host—once a native shell can host legacy RN screens as isolated leaves, every remaining screen can be replaced and verified independently. And when designing your verification harness, remember to test the test entry point itself,
Release
build flags, real OS modal stacks, and async teardown across live runtime sessions.
I'm not a veteran iOS engineer, and this layering reflects how I reasoned through the problem rather than established orthodoxy. I'm still weighing trade-offs—like whether running a JS data runtime inside an offscreen WebView is worth it long-term, whether protocol injection via
LodyHost
is the cleanest way to handle platform side effects, or whether keeping App UI code in folders rather than SPM packages will hold up as the codebase grows. If you've been through a similar migration or would structure this differently, I'd love to hear your thoughts in the comments.

items.text: innei published: 十个月，给 LobeHub 换掉 Ant Design：向 Base UI 与 StyleX 的渐进式迁移
items.title: 十个月，给 LobeHub 换掉 Ant Design：向 Base UI 与 StyleX 的渐进式迁移
items.content:
The starting point: a performance tuning pass
During my first month at LobeHub, I ran a performance optimization pass, documented with benchmarks in
"Performance and DX Optimizations at LobeHub"
. The heaviest bottlenecks in that pass were all style-related: CSS-in-JS Flexbox components like react-layout-kit numbered in the hundreds on a single page, each generating CSS; the
useStyle
running across almost every component recalculated styles on every re-render; and a single antd Tooltip took 0.5ms on its own. The first two could be fixed by switching styling solutions, but Tooltip required a full rewrite. I rebuilt both it and Popover with Base UI—the first time Base UI was used in lobe-ui.
With those fixes in place, the remaining overhead came from antd components themselves. Since antd's UI was also notoriously hard to customize deeply, replacing it was the obvious next move. I had wanted to do this for a while, but never started because manually rewriting a codebase of this size was unrealistic, and AI wasn't capable enough yet.
When we actually started, this was what we were facing:
@lobehub/ui
had almost a hundred component modules, with behavior tightly coupled to antd and all component styles written in Emotion-based
antd-style
, which generated CSS at runtime and injected it into the document on every page load. Downstream, five ecosystem libraries—icons, editor, charts, tts, and fluent-emoji—declared it as a peer dependency, and at the top layer, hundreds of business files in lobe-chat directly imported from
import ... from 'antd'
. Meanwhile, product features shipped weekly, so maintaining a long-running rewrite branch wasn't an option. The entire migration had to happen without interrupting delivery, split into two parallel tracks: first swap out the underlying component foundation from antd to Base UI, then switch styling from runtime Emotion to compile-time StyleX.
Letting old and new components coexist in the same package
lobe-ui#448
rewrote Tooltip. Beyond performance gains, it also resolved seven Linear issues: positioning drift, tooltips failing to dismiss, and elements snapping back to (0, 0) when their host unmounted. Base UI is headless, providing only behavior and accessibility while leaving DOM structure and styling to us, so we could customize everything freely without fighting antd's limitations.
The next question was how to make the transition. With weekly product releases and several downstream libraries tracking our changes, ripping out antd all at once wasn't practical. Instead, I opted for coexistence: build new components with Base UI, package them alongside the antd versions, and migrate product call sites one component at a time. Throughout January 2026, we gradually added
lobe-ui#444
's Base UI Menu–based DropdownMenu and ContextMenu, alongside LobeSwitch and LobeSelect. To avoid name clashes with their antd counterparts, they initially carried a Lobe prefix or a V2 suffix.
On March 2,
lobe-ui#467
released v5, formalizing this coexistence in the package structure: adding a
@lobehub/ui/base-ui
subpath where LobeSelect and LobeSwitch were moved (dropping their prefixes), while DropdownMenu, Toast, ContextMenu, and ScrollArea were exported from there as well. The package itself also became ESM-only. Subsequent components followed the exact same pattern: the implementation lived under
src/base-ui/
, while the root entry only re-exported it. For instance, when
lobe-ui#486
migrated Popover,
@lobehub/ui
and
@lobehub/ui/base-ui
were both valid, requiring zero changes in product code. From here on, migrating a component took just two steps: write the new implementation under base-ui, then switch the call sites in product code.
Components had to be drop-in replacements, locked down with linting once migrated
Between March and September, components were ported into base-ui roughly in this order: overlays, basic controls, forms, display, and layout.
Overlays first
This came down to two reasons. To begin with, overlays naturally belong together: Dropdown, Popover, Tooltip, Modal, and Drawer all share floating positioning and stacking management, making them ideal to tackle together. Later,
lobe-ui#518
unified their z-index management under a single layer manager. The second reason was how Modal was structured. Antd's Modal is primarily declarative, requiring components to be mounted on the React tree in advance:
open
is
false
, its children still render, re-rendering whenever ancestor state updates. With multiple Modals on a page, that overhead adds up on every single render. An imperative Modal creates an instance only when invoked and destroys it when closed, shifting the cost to the user action that opens it. I previously wrote about this in
"Why I Recommend Imperative Modals,"
and base-ui's Modal has supported both imperative and declarative patterns since its
first release
.
In the top example, every closed Modal participates in every render; in the bottom example, only the active Modal exists in the tree.
Migration windows by component category
After overlays came basic controls, forms, and display components. They all followed the exact same workflow: merge the new component into base-ui, switch product call sites over, and finally ban the legacy import via ESLint. Each bar below runs from when the new component merged to when the legacy import was banned:
A stark dividing line is visible around August. Before August, taking a component category from initial merge to banning legacy imports took weeks or months: Modal and Select took nearly four months, and form controls took 36 days. After August, Drawer took 5 days, Alert 6 days, Skeleton 3 days, DraggablePanel and Tree 2 days each, while ActionIcon, Avatar, Tag, and Text took just 1 day combined. The migration process hadn't changed—what changed was the models. Anthropic released Claude Fable 5 on June 9 and Claude Opus 5 on July 24. To me, Opus 5 felt exceptionally strong at front-end tasks, and at half the price of Fable 5, it cost about the same as Opus 4.8. By August, commits in lobe-chat switched from Opus 4.8 to Opus 5, and Fable 5 usage was rising too. The bars for Tabs and Segmented are also very short, but only because the initial preset banned five components all at once on June 26—not because they migrated faster.
Components like DropdownMenu, Tooltip, and Popover were replaced in place at the root entry point without legacy versions to ban, so they aren't shown in the chart. Commits for each component:
Modal
,
Menu
,
Tooltip
,
Button
,
Form controls
,
Drawer
,
Alert
,
ActionIcon and three others
,
Skeleton
,
DraggablePanel
, and
Tree
.
Each new component had to be a drop-in replacement, matching the old version in both API and visuals so switching only meant changing import paths. In lobe-ui#621, Tag's color resolution was ported straight from the old implementation: 13 preset colors, 5 system colors, and and all four variants (solid, filled, outlined, borderless) across three sizes had to match. Avatar replaced antd Avatar with native
img
, keeping the fallback on load failure and the +N counter for AvatarGroup. After Drawer merged, a separate
commit
followed to align its surface, edges, and drop shadows with antd Drawer.
The ban rules lived in lobe-ui's built-in ESLint preset, inherited directly by product projects. The
initial preset
on June 26 deprecated and banned imports of five antd-based wrappers: Button, Modal, Segmented, Select, and Tabs. When that first version went live, product code still had numerous legacy calls, which were temporarily grandfathered via an allowlist (detailed in the next section). From that point on, rules for each component category were added to the preset only after downstream projects had cleared all legacy imports. The PR description in
lobe-ui#610
was blunt: downstream migrations had removed legacy imports for these components, and this PR turned the migration boundary into an enforceable lint rule. That way, new code couldn't introduce old patterns, and legacy usage could only ever go down.
On the product side: freeze new usage, then clear legacy code category by category
Each time lobe-ui finished migrating a component category, lobe-chat had to update corresponding call sites. The chart below shows the number of files directly importing antd in lobe-chat, sampled biweekly:
Until mid-June, this line kept rising—climbing from 338 in mid-February to 485 on June 15. While legacy calls were being replaced, new features continued using antd. By then, the team had already delegated most product coding to AI, and component precedence had long been codified into
AGENTS.md
and react skills:
@lobehub/ui/base-ui
Any component available in it had to be imported from it, with same-named components at the root entry point off-limits, leaving antd strictly as a fallback when neither had it. Agents routinely ignored this. Because training data and hundreds of existing files demonstrated antd patterns, PRs for new features kept using legacy components even after lobe-ui published replacements. To an agent, docs are merely suggestions. The only way to stop them was to make violations break the build: ESLint fails directly, and lint-staged runs the same checks in pre-commit hooks to block the commit.
That was precisely what
lobehub#16334
did on June 26: it adopted lobe-ui's ESLint preset, banning the five legacy wrappers (Button, Modal, Segmented, Select, Tabs) as well as antd-style's
createStyles
; existing call sites (354 in total) were added to
eslint-suppressions.json
for temporary exemption, while any new violations failed immediately. Afterward, whenever a batch was migrated, we ran
eslint --prune-suppressions
, ensuring the allowlist only ever shrank.
Legacy code was cleared category by category: each PR targeted only one component category, but covered the entire repository. The count dropped slowly over the summer, followed by a steep drop in early October.
lobehub#20247
touched 285 files in one go, swapping out all remaining instances of Table, DatePicker, Menu, List, Input variants, and more, eliminating 163 files with direct antd imports. The PR included before-and-after screenshots compared against canary for verification, and five component library issues caught along the way were patched in
lobe-ui#675
. Next,
lobehub#20317
migrated forms, removing another 63 files;
lobehub#20408
updated menu item types to lobe-ui's, shedding 21 files; finally,
lobehub#20503
cleaned up the remainder. The two files still remaining on November 1 in the chart are test fixtures for alint.
Behavioral discrepancies are harder to catch than visual differences
Visual differences are easy to spot by comparing screenshots side by side, but behavioral discrepancies usually don't surface until a user saves data. After lobehub#20317 migrated forms to base-ui, the values returned on submit differed between the two:
antd Form
base-ui Form
Returned on submit
Values of currently mounted
Form.Item
fields only
Entire form store
Conditionally hidden fields
Discarded
Submitted together
initialValues
extra keys
Discarded
Submitted together
Fields that used to be quietly dropped were now persisted together. Switching a plugin's authentication from bearer to none left the old token behind. Similarly, switching transport from HTTP to stdio kept the old URL, causing later re-installations to fetch manifests from that stale address and overwrite existing settings.
lobehub#20644
added a
pruneHiddenFields
step before saving to prune fields that don't belong to the active type.
The compatibility layer itself can introduce bugs. The
ImperativeModal
wrapper, created for a smooth migration, unmounted its content in the very same commit that
open
became
false
, while base-ui's panel still had a 120ms exit animation—so closing the Skill Store details modal caused the content to collapse prematurely. Instead of patching the wrapper,
lobehub#17941
replaced all 11 call sites with imperative
createModal
Content lives inside a ModalHost and is only unmounted after the exit animation finishes.
Bumping the ecosystem libraries along with lobe-ui's majors
As we wrapped up the app-level cleanup, the intermediate ecosystem tier had to come along. Beyond lobe-ui, lobe-chat depends on icons, editor, charts, tts, and fluent-emoji—most of which declare lobe-ui as a peer dependency:
Whenever lobe-ui bumped a major version, the ecosystem layer broke: downstream packages lost exports they still needed, or peer versions fell out of sync. As a result, we always released them all together:
lobe-ui
Release date

v6 was by far the biggest set of changes, split into a stacked sequence of PRs:
lobe-ui#699
removed the antd components and
ThemeProvider
;
lobe-ui#700
dropped the antd, antd-style, and rc-* dependencies; and
lobe-ui#702
merged
src/base-ui
completely empty.
@lobehub/ui/base-ui
back into the root directory, getting rid of the base-ui subpath. With the coexistence phase over, we tore down that v5 scaffolding and exported the new components straight from the root entry. In early October, the downstream libraries first ported their own component usage over to base-ui (
lobe-editor#222
and
lobe-charts#32
), before each bumped to lobe-ui 6 and stripped out antd.
This cascade of changes couldn't be released and verified piecemeal. Instead, we tested across repos using pkg.pr.new preview packages: PRs for lobe-ui and the five downstream libraries each published preview packages, and
lobehub#20503
pointed all dependencies to those preview URLs. We compared lobe-chat against production page by page to ensure zero visual regressions before officially publishing in dependency order and and then switched back to real version numbers. PR #20503 alone updated imports across 2,728 files, purged antd from 24 workspace packages, and finally left
pnpm ls -r antd
with nothing to show.
Moving styles from runtime generation to build-time compilation
Dropping antd took care of components, but styles were still being generated at runtime. lobe-ui wrote its component styles in antd-style, built on Emotion: on page load, JavaScript generated CSS on the fly and inserted it into the page. The initial optimization pass replaced dynamic hooks with
createStaticStyles
, ensuring components no longer recomputed styles on every re-render. Yet the insertion step remained. In September,
lobehub#19066
pre-computed purely static calls at build time, slashing the time spent on styles during cold home page loads from ~56ms to ~28ms. The remaining ~14ms came from
insertRule
itself—an unavoidable cost as long as emotion was in the loop.

It's already been over two weeks since my last recap, so it's time to catch up on what's been happening lately.
Nyatabi Hits the App Store
Last time, I mentioned running into so many headaches after a trip that I decided to build an app. At the end of my last post, I wrote, "Musubicho is still in development and not finished yet." Less than two weeks later, I renamed it Nyatabi (喵旅) and officially launched it on the App Store. That said, I haven't even been the first one to really test it out in the wild. I'm such a homebody that even though a trip sparked the project, I haven't had the chance to use all its features myself yet. I just love building products—created purely out of passion.
It's live on the App Store now, and I put together a decent landing page for it. Feel free to check it out! (Though it's iOS-only for now.)
Nyatabi — your AI travel companion for iPhone
Plan with Musubi, explore together, split spending fairly and turn your route into memories. Your whole journey, in one local-first iPhone app.
Nyatabi
Beyond helping you map out trips, it lets an agent handle expense tracking and bill splitting on the go (either by snapping receipts or just telling it what you spent). In group chats, the agent can scout nearby restaurants or pull up your friends' locations. And once the trip wraps up, you can replay your route, generate an auto-edited highlight video, or export a detailed travel footprint report.
Before the official release, I shot a 4-part short video series walking through the entire flow: pre-trip planning → snapping receipts to split expenses on the go → settling balances with minimum transfers → everyday roommate bookkeeping. On October 16, I posted a full 2-minute demo.
Along the way, I also open-sourced the rounded-line icon set used in Nyatabi at
icons.nyatabi.app
.
Engineering shortcuts vs. engineering rigor: refusing to be a human test runner, I wired up XCUITest across two physical iPhones so agents could handle the entire closed loop of "implement → verify → fail → fix" on their own (check out my technical post, "
My AI-Native iOS Development & Verification Workflow
", for details).
It could be handy whether you're traveling or just going about everyday life: I've always found life-logging footprint apps a bit awkward to use, so I baked my own footprint features right in to track daily routines as well. I don't want to turn this into a full-on product pitch, so I'll stop here. If you're interested, feel free to give it a spin.
Nyatabi: AI Travel Planner App - App Store

AI in the Trenches
A Love-Hate Relationship with Claude
I had a backup Claude alt account that managed to hold out for over two weeks, so I decided to upgrade it. Went from Pro to Max, only to get slapped with an instant ban—no refund, either. I was so anxious that night that I stayed up by myself until 5 a.m. Eventually, I couldn't help setting up yet another account, and that one's somehow still alive.
On top of that, my $DRAM shares kept tumbling before I could break even, so those days felt like a brutal double blow from Anthropic and $DRAM. It also got me calculating the real cost of compute inflation: last year, a $20 Claude subscription felt like it could do so much; now, even the $200 Max tier barely scratches the surface. By comparison, Apple's $99/year developer membership is so cheap it's almost moving.
OpenAI's "God Tier" Account and Kimi Falling Flat on Its Face
There was a funny little detour along the way. Around the 20th, I noticed a bug in OpenAI: an old 20x subscription was still usable even after downgrading or canceling. I honestly thought I'd struck gold with some chosen "god-tier" account. But by day five of freeloading, the bug got patched and my quota went straight to zero.
Then on the 23rd, I dropped $19 on Kimi, wanting to see how it compared to $20 Claude. I asked it to write a website footer—and before it even finished, barely ten minutes in, I slammed right into a 5-hour rate limit. Might as well just call yourselves QueueShot AI. When it comes to domestic models, everyone should just use DeepSeek—what are the rest of these garbage knockoffs even doing? DeepSeek is the only one that can actually play: no token sales, no bullshit. The API pricing is right there: take it or leave it. The TPS is right there too—DeepSeek 4.1 Flash pushes over 200 TPS, and at those prices, burn through as much as you want.
Unlike Kimi—their greed this time is honestly shameless: zero compute power, but pulling that classic Lei Jun artificial scarcity playbook and taking users for fools to the extreme.
Ryugi (流儀) — Open-Source Claude Artifacts
After getting jerked around like that, I thought: why not just build my own version of Claude Artifacts? I genuinely love using that feature. For docs, artboard designs, and architecture sketches, it's just so damn good—a product genuinely made with care.
But being locked into Claude's proprietary subscription was a dealbreaker. So what choice did I have? Build it myself.
Claude Artifacts support five types, and the ones I use most are Artboard, Document, and HTML. Sick of taking Anthropic's nonsense, I cobbled together a standalone workbench called "Ryugi" (
ryugi.innei.dev
).
Building this brought an unexpected bonus too: it completely changed my view of Codex's design skills. I used to think Codex was garbage at design, and just on the 10th I had tweeted about how miserable it was trying to write UI with it. But once I plugged it into Ryugi's Artboard workflow, it turned out to be surprisingly solid—I guess I was just using it wrong before. To my surprise, that tweet blew up, racking up 93K impressions and over 700 bookmarks.
I've been using it for a few days now, putting it through heavy daily use and constantly refining it. The cloud environment is live too, so now it helps me brainstorm, work on designs, hash out architecture docs, and even knock out small feature requests on the side.
The experience genuinely captures the vibe of Claude Artifacts now. Hooking this workflow up to other harnesses—like DeepSeek or Codex—makes them dramatically more useful. If you haven't tried it yet, you really should.

LobeHub Bids Farewell to AntD
On the work front: I've been here for almost a year now. Back when I first joined, I declared that I was going to ditch AntD once and for all. That turned into a ten-month marathon, but on the 9th of this month, I finally pulled it off—migrating everything over to
@base_ui
+
StyleX
(meaning
lobe-ui
v6).
Looking back at the numbers, the engineering scale was pretty wild:
lobe-ui
rewrote 54 components on top of Base UI, and AntD dependencies in
lobe-editor
,
lobe-charts
, and
lobe-icons
were completely eliminated.
The main repo has over 11,000 TypeScript files. Replacing the underlying component library spanned 28 PRs and touched 3,242 files, with the single largest PR modifying 1,040 files.
Along the way, we also migrated our CSS-in-JS setup to StyleX, slashing the original 179 emotion files down to just 3. The most satisfying part was running 5 agents across parallel branches: in three and a half hours, they plowed through 84 commits. We then ran regression tests across 45 routes using 1,000 screenshot comparisons and computed-style diffs, reliably catching 4 regressions.
Getting rid of AntD paid off right away. Bundle sizes shrank dramatically, and pages feel noticeably snappier. Thinking back, before AI agents existed, a core refactor of this scale would have easily taken an entire team a full quarter of grinding. But with today's models being so capable, I managed to knock out this massive project almost entirely on my own.
The Story Ends Here
Throughout October, blind dates from family and friends were nonstop, but most of the time chatting was pretty draining. Earlier in the month, I tweeted a rant saying some WeChat chats feel like "an LLM running on a potato server, taking hours of inference just to spit out a few characters, and if you don't send a request, you'll never get a response." That tweet unexpectedly racked up over 70,000 views, and predictably enough, I got hit with the "you're a nice guy" card in real life soon after.
But just a few days later, through another blind date, I unexpectedly met someone I could genuinely click with—something that hadn't happened in a long time.
I find myself wanting deeper conversations lately—talking about fundamental values, life outlooks, and thoughts on the future. In day-to-day life, finding someone who can actually match that energy is rare. But that night—which also happened to be our last conversation—we talked about so much. Beyond having plenty of shared interests, what hit hardest was a real resonance in who we are deep down. Just knowing someone on that exact same wavelength actually exists was a wonderful, lucky surprise.
Unfortunately, she felt our personalities were just too similar to be a good match. In the end, we parted ways gracefully, and that was where the story ended.
Turning My Resume into a Canvas
Another project I spent a lot of time on was completely rebuilding my personal resume page for Programmer's Day on October 24, launching it at
resume.innei.in/lab/
.
The spark was simple: surfing online recently, I saw a few personal sites and resumes that looked amazing, so I wanted to bring my own ideas into the mix and polish up something of my own. A traditional single-page format can't hold very much, so I turned it into a canvas you can freely pan, zoom, and explore—connecting all the projects I've worked on and milestones I've reached over the six or seven years since college into one continuous timeline.
Working on this canvas also ended up unlocking some new skills. To give the page some fitting background music, I dove into arranging with realistic virtual instruments, tweaking synthesis, and fine-tuning the details (huge thanks to
@wibus_wee
for walking me through Ozone mastering), and I even built an interactive sheet music display into the canvas.
Cramming a bunch of music arrangement and audio mastering just to build a resume was an unexpected bonus. Once I get around to picking music theory back up properly, I really should build an app for instruments and music theory.
Thanks for reading this far.
Also, I recently updated the background on this blog with dynamic nature scenes that change with the seasons and time of day. I even split the effect out into its own standalone preview page (
innei.in/dev-demos/backgrounds
); if you're interested, feel free to click in and play around with it.
